The Spell of the Yukon
Robert W. Service (1907) · from “The Spell of the Yukon,” stanza 1
· · ·
I wanted the gold, and I sought it, I scrabbled and mucked like a slave. Was it famine or scurvy—I fought it; I hurled my youth into a grave. I wanted the gold, and I got it— Came out with a fortune last fall,— Yet somehow life's not what I thought it, And somehow the gold isn't all.
· · ·
scrabbled: scratched and dug in a hurry · mucked: shoveled dirt and gravel · famine: a time of terrible hunger · scurvy: a sickness from too little fresh food

✏️ Daily Oral Language
Study the model, then fix the sentence.
✅ Model
The stranger shut the crate, and Buck heard the latch fall.

Buck is a name, so it takes a capital letter. Two complete sentences joined by and take a comma before the and.

🔧 Fix this one
the rope tightened around his neck and buck fought the stranger
Rewrite it correctly.
🔍 Check my work

The rope tightened around his neck, and Buck fought the stranger. The sentence opens with a capital, Buck is a name, and a comma comes before and because two complete sentences are joined. It ends with a period.

1
🍎 At the Board with Professor Lovelore
Verbs, subjects, and the words that receive the action
Professor Lovelore At the board
1:15
An AI-generated character and voice.
Verb, then subject
What is being said about the subject? That is the verb.
Who or what does it? That is the subject noun.
Manuel→subject nounsold→verb
Direct object
Subject, verb, what or whom?
Manuel sold Buck.
Sold what? Buck. It receives the action.
Indirect object
Verb, direct object, to whom or for whom?
The man gave Buck a lesson.
gave what?→a lessonto whom?→Buck
1. No direct, no indirect
An indirect object needs a direct object in the same sentence.
2. After in, into, with
Buck rode in the express car.
car is the object of the preposition, not a direct object.

LabelWhat it doesExample
subject noundoes the actionPerrault grinned.
verbwhat is being said about the subjectPerrault grinned.
article adjectivepoints to a nouna, an, the
direct objectreceives the actionFrançois leashed the dogs.
indirect objectwho or what the direct object goes toMollie handed the Judge a letter.
object of the prepositionends a phrase that begins with a word like in, into, or withBuck slept beside the fire.

🪶 Read like a Reader, Read like a Writer, Mimic
One sentence from Chapter I, three ways.
“He was beaten (he knew that); but he was not broken.”Jack London · The Call of the Wild, Chapter I
📖 Read like a Reader

What does the sentence say Buck knew, and what does it say he was not? What kind of character thinks that way?

✏️ Read like a Writer

London tucks he knew that inside parentheses and joins the two halves with a semicolon. What does each mark do to the way you read the sentence?

🖊️ Mimic

Write a sentence in the same shape about a different character: a clause, a quiet aside in parentheses, a semicolon, then a second clause that pushes back on the first.

___ was ___ (___ knew that); but ___ was not ___.

Your draft: two parts, 150 to 200 words
  1. Before: show your subject before the change, with details a reader can picture.
  2. After: show what is different, with new details.
  3. The cause: end with one sentence that names what caused the change. Someone could disagree with it.

🔎 Watch your verbs

A strong action verb with a clear direct object does more work than a weak one.

🪶 Sentence frames you can borrow

Before: ___ was ___. I could see ___ and ___.

After: Now ___. The ___ had ___, and ___ was gone.

The cause: ___ did more to ___ than ___.

📖 Mateo’s draft, a model
Mateo
7th Grade Scholar · the creek behind our building

Before the flood, the creek behind our building was the best part of summer. The water ran clear over flat stones, and when I knelt on the bank I could count the minnows darting through the shallows. On the big sycamore hung a rope swing, and every afternoon my cousins and I swung out over the water and dropped in with a shout. The creek felt small and friendly, like a neighbor who always waved.

After the flood, I hardly knew the place. The water was brown and thick, full of broken branches that bumped along the banks. Part of the bank had caved in, leaving a raw wall of dirt where we used to sit. The rope swing was gone, and only a frayed knot was left on the sycamore. Even the sound was different: the creek no longer chattered; it growled. One night of flood did more to the creek than ten quiet summers.
